problem: Prior VLN agents rely on recurrent policies, which struggle with long-term dependencies and long trajectories. High-level (panoramic, graph-teleport) methods lean on simulator connectivity knowledge and lose performance when moved to atomic low-level actions, so they adapt poorly to real-world locomotion.
motivation: Low-level VLN (turn, tilt, step forward) is closer to real robot control, but few works address it. Success requires fusing language, vision and action history, and the authors observe that a fully attentive model can infer agent state directly from observations without recurrence, generalize to longer episodes, and be agnostic to the action space.
key_idea: PTA is a recurrence-free Transformer-like VLN agent that fuses instruction and panoramic vision early in the encoder, then fuses the action history with both modalities late in the decoder, and can swap its output head between low-level and high-level action spaces.
insight: Ablations show every attention component matters: removing early text-vision cross-attention drops val-unseen SPL from 0.32 to 0.20, and keeping only the last action instead of the full history drops SR from 0.39 to 0.22. Vision is essential (a blind, text-only agent gets SR 0.03-0.04), and the text-action branch mainly helps unseen generalization. Retraining high-level baselines with a low-level head drops SR by 11% (Speaker-Follower) and 13% (Self-Monitoring), versus a small gap for PTA (0.40 vs 0.43 SR). This suggests high-level gains partly come from the simpler action space.
method: Instruction encoder: stop-word filtering, GloVe, linear projection with LayerNorm, sinusoidal positional encoding, multi-head self-attention and feed-forward (d_model 512, 8 heads).

Image encoder: 360° panorama split into a 3x12 grid (36 regions), ResNet-152 features with (sin φ, cos φ, sin θ) coordinates, self-attention, then cross-attention with the instruction as keys/values (early fusion), then feed-forward.
Action-history decoder: past actions (one-hot, starting with a <start> token) with positional encoding pass through self-attention in place of an RNN.

Late fusion multimodal decoder: two cross-attention branches with the history as query, one over visual features and one over text features. Their outputs are concatenated and passed through an FC layer, and the last element is used.

Action selection: a softmax over 6 actions (turn left/right 30°, tilt up/down, forward, end). For high-level mode, the softmax is replaced by a bilinear similarity between the state s_t and navigable viewpoint features.

Training: imitation learning (cross-entropy on shortest-path actions) with Speaker synthetic data augmentation, followed by fine-tuning on human data only. Then REINFORCE fine-tuning with an nDTW-gain step reward plus an episode-level success reward max(0, 1 - d_goal/d_th).

setting.backbone: PTA: attention-based Transformer-like encoder-decoder (GloVe + ImageNet ResNet-152 features), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: R2R train set plus Fried et al. Speaker synthetic instructions for pretraining (then fine-tuned on R2R human data only); R4R train for the R4R experiments
setting.observation: panoramic 360° RGB (36-region grid, ResNet-152 features) plus instruction
setting.action_space: low-level: turn left/right 30°, tilt up/down, step forward, end episode (also a high-level nav-graph variant)
setting.privileged: none for the low-level agent (the high-level variant uses the navigation connectivity graph)

results: On the R2R test server PTA reaches SR 0.40 and SPL 0.36 in low-level VLN, beating the previous best low-level method (Landi et al., SR 0.35, SPL 0.31) by about 5 points. On R4R it beats the low-level baseline (val-unseen CLS 0.35 vs 0.33) and is competitive with the high-level baselines. High-level PTA is weaker than the best high-level R2R methods (e.g. SPL 0.53).
limitations: Absolute performance in low-level VLN is still far below that of high-level methods, and the comparison is not direct.
The paper reports only simulator results with a fixed 6-action space; there is no real-robot or continuous control.
Baselines were re-adapted for the action-space switch (only Speaker-Follower and Self-Monitoring), so the adaptability claim rests on a limited set of comparisons.
